blocks.passage:
Most professionals write more emails in a year than anything else they will ever write. Yet very few have ever been trained in how to write them well. The result is the inbox many of us live in — long, vague, hard to answer.

A good email does three things quickly: it tells the reader what it is about, what is expected of them, and by when. The first line should answer the question "Why am I reading this?" The last line should answer the question "What do I do now?"

Tone also matters. Emails are read faster than they are written, and subtle things — word choice, length, punctuation — shape the reader's reaction more than we realise. When in doubt, shorter, calmer and clearer always wins.

items.q: What does the text say most professionals lack?
options: Training in how to write emails well
items.why: "very few have ever been trained in how to write them well."

items.q: What three things does a good email do quickly?
options: Copy everyone, attach a file and sign off
Say what it is about, what is expected, and by when
items.why: "it tells the reader what it is about, what is expected of them, and by when."

items.q: According to the text, the first line should answer…
items.why: "The first line should answer the question 'Why am I reading this?'"

items.q: The last line should answer…
items.why: "The last line should answer the question 'What do I do now?'"

items.q: What is the author's overall advice when unsure about an email?
options: Add more detail to be safe
items.why: "When in doubt, shorter, calmer and clearer always wins."

audio.text:
Okay, I've read your draft to the client, and the content is fine — it's just buried. Let me talk you through the changes I'd make.

Right now the subject line just says "Update". The client gets a hundred emails a day, so I've changed it to "Delivery date confirmed — action needed by Thursday". They know what it's about and that something is expected of them before they even open it.

The first paragraph had three sentences of background before the point. I've moved the point up: "We can confirm delivery for the twelfth; we need your sign-off on the final spec by Thursday." Background can come after.

I've also cut the email roughly in half. Two of the paragraphs were really just thinking out loud. And I've softened one line — "you failed to send the spec" became "we haven't received the spec yet". Same fact, better tone.

Last thing: the old version buried the request in the middle. I've put it on its own line at the end, so there's no way to miss what to do next.

items.q: What does Charlotte say about the content of the draft?
items.why: "the content is fine — it's just buried."

items.q: Why did she rewrite the subject line?
options: So the client knows the topic and that action is expected before opening
items.why: "They know what it's about and that something is expected of them before they even open it."

items.q: What did she do with the main point of the first paragraph?
options: Moved it to the subject line
Moved it up, ahead of the background
items.why: "I've moved the point up… Background can come after."

items.q: Why did she change "you failed to send the spec"?
options: To keep the same fact but a better tone
items.why: "'you failed to send the spec' became 'we haven't received the spec yet'. Same fact, better tone."

items.q: What is Charlotte's reason for putting the request on its own line at the end?
options: So there is no way to miss what to do next
items.why: "so there's no way to miss what to do next."

items.q: "Most readers **skim** a long email rather than read every word." To skim means to…
options: read quickly for the main points
items.why: To skim = ler por cima, buscando o essencial.

items.q: The **subject line** is…
options: the short heading that tells the reader what the email is about
items.why: Subject line = linha de assunto.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "End with a clear ___ so the reader knows exactly what to do."
items.why: Call to action = chamada para ação: o que o leitor deve fazer.

items.q: "Please keep the message **concise**." Concise means…
items.why: Concise = conciso, curto e claro.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "I'll ___ next week to see if you need anything else."
items.why: Circle back = retomar o contato mais tarde.

items.q: "I'll **follow up** on this by Friday." To follow up means to…
items.why: Follow up = dar sequência.

items.q: "Let me **flag** one risk before we send." To flag something means to…
items.why: To flag = sinalizar, chamar atenção para um ponto.

items.q: "Please **loop in** legal on this thread." To loop someone in means to…
items.why: Loop in = incluir alguém na conversa (geralmente em cópia).

items.q: "Can you **CC** me on the reply?" To CC someone means to…
options: send them a copy visible to all recipients
items.why: CC (carbon copy) = copiar de forma visível; BCC é a cópia oculta.

items.q: "Let's not **reply-all** — only the two of us need this." Reply-all means to…
items.why: Reply-all = responder a todos; aqui, evitável porque só duas pessoas precisam.
